---
title: "Classifying Texts with tidyllm"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE)
options(width = 90)
```

You have thousands of short free-text answers and a fixed list of categories. A language model can sort them in minutes, but a label is only as good as the check behind it. **tidyllm** gives you two ways to ask a model about them.

With `chat()`, the model writes a reply; with `decide()`, it answers a closed question and returns a probability. A closed question has fixed possible answers, such as your list of 23 occupation codes; the probability is the model's score for its chosen answer, from 0 to 1. See the [decision models article](https://edubruell.github.io/tidyllm/articles/tidyllm_decision_models.html) for other question types.

This article builds a workflow with a codebook, one closed question per answer using `decide()`, a look at the probabilities, a second provider, and three repeated `chat()` runs for comparison. It then uses a `chat()` pass with a written reason for doubtful rows, followed by a human-labelled sample.

The second provider and the `chat()` pass are optional; the codebook and human sample are not. Agreement is not accuracy. Agreement between models shows where they are unsure; only comparison with human labels shows whether they are right.

Every call that needs an API key appears in a chunk that is not evaluated. The next chunk loads the saved result and prints it, so you can follow the measured results without making a live call.

A provider is the company whose server runs the model; an API key is a password that lets your R session use it. `decide()` needs one key for the provider you choose: `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `GOOGLE_API_KEY` or `TYPESAFE_API_KEY`. The key table in [Get Started](https://edubruell.github.io/tidyllm/articles/tidyllm.html) says where to get each one.

## The task

Seven thousand survey respondents described their job in their own words. We want each answer in one of the 22 two-digit SOC occupation groups, or in code 99 when the answer names no occupation.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(tidyllm)
library(tidyverse)
library(glue)

occ_data  <- read_rds("occupation_data.rds")
occ_codes <- read_rds("occ_codes_2digits.rds")

distinct_occupations <- occ_data |>
  distinct(occupation = occupation_open) |>
  mutate(id = row_number())

print(distinct_occupations, n = 5)
```

Classifying each distinct answer once is enough; the labels are joined back to the respondents at the end. Among the 7,000 respondents, there are 2,209 distinct answers to classify.

## Why a single answer is not enough

Studies of LLM annotation find that repeated runs of the same prompt on the same text return different labels, especially for borderline texts (Barrie, Palaiologou and Törnberg, 2024; Haldar and Hockenmaier, 2025). An LLM label is only as good as its agreement with humans on your task (Pangakis, Wolken and Fasching, 2023).

## Two ways to ask a model

A *decision model* answers closed questions with an answer and a probability and writes no text. Its probability is its own score, from 0 to 1: a high score means strong preference, not a promise of being right nine times in ten. Step 3 checks how well scores match reality; the [decision models article](https://edubruell.github.io/tidyllm/articles/tidyllm_decision_models.html) covers yes/no, choice and score questions.

This article runs `openai()`, `gemini()` and `jev()`, a small model service from TypeSafe AI built for this kind of task; see the provider table in the [decision models article](https://edubruell.github.io/tidyllm/articles/tidyllm_decision_models.html). `ollama()` also works as a decision provider; the decision models article shows how.

| Job | Use | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Sort texts into a fixed list of labels | `decide()` | one call gives a label and a probability, in about 0.2 seconds |
| Screen texts with yes/no questions | `decide()` | one probability per question |
| Score a text on an ordered scale | `decide()` with an ordered question | the scale order is the level order |
| Write a reason, a summary or a free label | `chat()` | `decide()` returns no text |
| Work with a PDF, image or file | `chat()` | `chat()` accepts files and images; `decide()` takes one piece of text per call |
| Decide a hard case after thinking | `chat()` | a reasoning model works through the problem step by step before it answers; it is slower and costs more |

For a hard case, switch reasoning on with `.thinking = TRUE` in the provider call, as Step 5 does.

## Step 1: Write a codebook, not a list

A bare list of codes leaves the model to guess what "Management" or "Missing" means. A codebook gives each label a definition, a decision rule for overlaps, and one or two examples. A human coder would need the same thing.

```{r codebook}
codebook <- read_file("classifier_codebook.txt") |> trimws()
cat(codebook)
```

Keep the codebook in a file under version control. When you change it, you have changed the measurement, and the validation in step 6 has to be run again. The last section of this article shows what happens when you edit the codebook to fix the errors you found. We use the codebook twice: as the level descriptions in Step 2 and as the prompt in Step 5.

## Step 2: Turn the codebook into a question

In R, a choice question is a factor, and its possible answers are called levels. Each level here is an occupation code with a one-sentence description from the codebook. The file has one line per code, with the code first and its definition after it.

We split each line into `code` and `description`. The `extra = "merge"` setting keeps everything after the first space in the description.

```{r codebook_levels}
codebook_lines <- read_lines("classifier_codebook.txt") |>
  keep(\(x) nzchar(trimws(x)))

codebook_levels <- tibble(line = codebook_lines) |>
  separate(line, c("code", "description"), sep = " ", extra = "merge")
```

`field_fct()` takes the codes as `.levels` and their definitions as `.level_descriptions`. The model reads the descriptions, and the returned answer is a code. The 22 occupation groups plus code 99 make 23 levels.

```{r occ_questions}
occ_questions <- tidyllm_schema(
  name = "occupation_label",
  occ2 = field_fct(
    "The SOC two-digit occupation group of this survey answer.",
    .levels             = codebook_levels$code,
    .level_descriptions = codebook_levels$description
  )
)
```

```{r check_levels}
nrow(codebook_levels)
```

Check that `nrow(codebook_levels)` is 23. Then inspect the table to confirm that the descriptions match the codebook text.

`decide()` takes the text to judge in `.state`, the questions in `.questions`, and a provider. We put one framing line before the answer to tell the model what it is reading: "Survey question: What is your job? Answer: Residential roofer." Then we send that text and the occupation question to `gemini()`.

```{r frame_answer}
frame_answer <- \(x) paste0("Survey question: What is your job? Answer: ", x)
```

```{r decide_one, eval = FALSE}
decide(frame_answer("Residential roofer"), occ_questions, gemini())
```

```
# A tibble: 1 × 5
  question type   answer probability score
  <chr>    <chr>  <chr>        <dbl> <dbl>
1 occ2     choice 47           0.998    NA
```

The result has five columns: `question`, `type`, `answer`, `probability` and `score`. For `occ2`, the model chooses code 47, Construction and Extraction, which fits a roofer, and assigns it probability 0.998. `score` is `NA` because this choice question is not an ordered scale question.

Code 99 is the codebook's "Missing" category: the answer names no occupation, or is too vague to place. The framing line tells the model what kind of text it is reading.

> ⚠️ **Note:** Say in one line what the text is. Without it, `openai()` labelled 27 of 60 answers as 99 and reached 0.57; with it 0.87.

`gemini()` scored 0.83 both ways; we tried one wording of the line. Without the line, `openai()` labelled answers such as "Doctor" as 99, although the answer names a codable occupation.

A dry run builds the request `tidyllm` would send and stops before sending it, so you can check the codebook and text first. Set `.dry_run = TRUE`; it needs no API key. The [decision models article](https://edubruell.github.io/tidyllm/articles/tidyllm_decision_models.html) explains dry runs further.

```{r dry_run}
request <- decide(frame_answer("Doctor"), occ_questions, jev(), .dry_run = TRUE)
request$url
request$body$data$state
head(request$body$data$questions$occ2$criteria, 2)
```

Check `state` for the text being sent. The `criteria` list contains all 23 codes, each beside its description; the output shows the first two. This lets you confirm the codebook text reached the request before making a live call.

Because `decide()` handles one text per call, we wrap one answer in a small function, then use `map()` to apply it to each answer. `unnest()` unpacks the returned label and probability into separate columns.

```{r label_one}
label_one <- function(answer, provider) {
  res <- decide(frame_answer(answer), occ_questions, provider)
  tibble(label = res$answer, probability = res$probability)
}
```

```{r three_answers, eval = FALSE}
answers <- c("Residential roofer", "Keep things organized", "Barster")

tibble(occupation = answers) |>
  mutate(res = map(occupation, label_one, provider = gemini())) |>
  unnest(res)
```

```
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  occupation            label probability
  <chr>                 <chr>       <dbl>
1 Residential roofer    47          0.998
2 Keep things organized 99          0.806
3 Barster               35          0.882
```

The model assigns the roofer code 47, matching the human label. It assigns "Keep things organized" code 99 with probability 0.806 (the human label is 43); "Barster" receives code 35 (the human label is 99).

We check a random 60 of the 150 human-labelled answers, using seed 2026 and the saved `classifier_sample.rds` and `classifier_gold.rds` files. Sequential means one call after another: 60 answers took 12.0 seconds with `jev()` and 15.6 seconds with `gemini()`. At this sample size, one standard error is 4.6 percentage points.

```{r sample_items}
sample_df <- read_rds("classifier_sample.rds")
gold      <- read_rds("classifier_gold.rds")

set.seed(2026)
items <- sample_df |>
  inner_join(gold, by = "id") |>
  slice_sample(n = 60)
```

```{r run_gemini, eval = FALSE}
items |>
  mutate(res = map(occupation, label_one, provider = gemini())) |>
  unnest(res)
```

The same call runs with `openai()` and `jev()`; the saved results for all three providers are loaded below. This keeps the measured results available without making new calls when you build the article.

```{r run_all, eval = FALSE}
run_provider <- function(provider) {
  items |>
    mutate(res = map(occupation, label_one, provider = provider)) |>
    unnest(res)
}

decide_runs <- list(
  openai = run_provider(openai()),
  gemini = run_provider(gemini()),
  jev    = run_provider(jev())
)
write_rds(decide_runs, "classifier_decide_runs.rds")
```

```{r load_decide_runs}
decide_runs <- read_rds("classifier_decide_runs.rds")
```

## Step 3: Read the probability

For comparison, we use labels from three Claude Sonnet 5.5 runs per answer and take the majority, the label chosen most often. Step 5 shows how those labels were made. The table compares first-pass accuracy across providers and the Claude majority: `openai()` and `jev()` each get 52 of 60 right (0.867), while `gemini()` and Claude get 50 of 60 (0.833).

```{r first_pass}
claude_majority <- read_rds("classifier_runs.rds") |>
  filter(!is.na(label)) |>
  count(id, label) |>
  group_by(id) |>
  slice_max(n, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(id, majority = label)

claude_row <- items |>
  inner_join(claude_majority, by = "id") |>
  summarise(
    provider = "claude, majority of 3 runs",
    answers  = n(),
    correct  = sum(majority == gold),
    accuracy = round(mean(majority == gold), 3)
  )

decide_runs |>
  bind_rows(.id = "provider") |>
  group_by(provider) |>
  summarise(answers = n(), correct = sum(label == gold), accuracy = round(mean(label == gold), 3)) |>
  bind_rows(claude_row)
```

The table compares accuracy across probability bands for each provider. Each cell gives the share of answers labelled correctly, followed by the number of answers in that band; for example `0.96 (23)`; empty bands are shown as "0 rows".

```{r bands}
decide_runs |>
  bind_rows(.id = "provider") |>
  mutate(band = cut(probability, c(0, 0.5, 0.8, 0.95, 1), include.lowest = TRUE)) |>
  group_by(provider, band) |>
  summarise(cell = str_glue("{sprintf('%.2f', mean(label == gold))} ({n()})"), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = provider, values_from = cell, values_fill = "0 rows")
```

We use 0.8 as a round cut-off. Rows below it were right 60 to 70 percent of the time, rows at or above it 90 to 92 percent. A row below 0.8 is flagged, meaning marked for a second look; use its probability to prioritise human or model review.

```{r flagged}
decide_runs |>
  bind_rows(.id = "provider") |>
  mutate(flagged = probability < 0.8) |>
  group_by(provider, flagged) |>
  summarise(items = n(), correct = sum(label == gold), accuracy = round(mean(label == gold), 2), .groups = "drop")
```

A probability is *calibrated* when it matches how often the answer is right (Guo et al., 2017). Above 0.95, match rates were 96% for `gemini()` (23 rows), 100% for `jev()` (23 rows) and 92% for `openai()` (39 rows); between 0.5 and 0.8, rates were 60 to 69% across 16, 13 and 10 rows. Check calibration on your own data with the validation sample in Step 6.

In the `chat()` route the model writes a confidence word as one more field; `decide()` returns a number the provider computes for each answer.

A language model can give different answers when you ask twice. We asked each provider the same 20 questions twice. `openai()` and `gemini()` gave exactly the same answer and probability every time, 20 of 20. `jev()` gave the same label 19 times out of 20; its probability differed between the two calls in 14 of the 20 answers, by at most 0.11. For `jev()`, repeated calls give a spread; for the other two, ask another provider for a second opinion.

## Step 4: Ask a second decision model

Agreement is the share of answers where two providers choose the same code. The table compares the three pairs: `openai()` and `gemini()` agree on 0.92 of answers, `openai()` and `jev()` on 0.85, and `gemini()` and `jev()` on 0.87.

```{r agreement}
labels_wide <- decide_runs |>
  bind_rows(.id = "provider") |>
  pivot_wider(id_cols = c(id, occupation, gold), names_from = provider, values_from = label)

tibble(
  pair      = c("openai and gemini", "openai and jev", "gemini and jev"),
  agreement = c(
    mean(labels_wide$openai == labels_wide$gemini),
    mean(labels_wide$openai == labels_wide$jev),
    mean(labels_wide$gemini == labels_wide$jev)
  ) |> round(2)
)
```

All three agreed on 49 of the 60 answers; on those 49, 94 percent matched the human label.

```{r all_agree}
labels_wide |>
  filter(openai == gemini, gemini == jev) |>
  summarise(answers = n(), correct = sum(openai == gold), accuracy = round(mean(openai == gold), 3))
```

The providers also agree on two answers that do not match the human labels. All three assign "Barster" code 35 and "Loundry Worker" code 37; the human labels are 99 and 51, respectively.

```{r agree_examples}
labels_wide |>
  filter(occupation %in% c("Barster", "Loundry Worker")) |>
  select(occupation, openai, gemini, jev, human = gold)
```

The providers disagree on 11 of the 60 answers. The flag marks a row when any provider's probability is below 0.8 or their labels differ; it marks 23 of the 60 answers, including every disagreement. Flagged rows are marked for a second look.

```{r flag}
flags <- decide_runs |>
  bind_rows(.id = "provider") |>
  group_by(id) |>
  summarise(
    low_probability  = any(probability < 0.8),
    providers_differ = n_distinct(label) > 1,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(flagged = low_probability | providers_differ)

flags |>
  summarise(
    low_probability  = sum(low_probability),
    providers_differ = sum(providers_differ),
    flagged          = sum(flagged),
    differ_not_flagged = sum(providers_differ & !flagged)
  )
```

## Step 5: Send the doubtful rows to `chat()`

For flagged rows, we want a written reason from a stronger model that thinks before answering. `decide()` returns no text; the schema `occ_schema` below makes `chat()` return a structured reply with a label, reason and confidence word.

A reasoning model works through the problem before it answers and costs more per call, so we use it only on doubtful rows marked for review. Step 6 reports the accuracy of both routes.

```{r schema}
label_levels <- as.character(c(occ_codes$occ2, 99)) |> unique()

occ_schema <- tidyllm_schema(
  name       = "occupation_label",
  rationale  = field_chr("One sentence: which words in the answer decide the group."),
  occ2       = field_fct("The SOC two-digit group from the codebook.", .levels = label_levels),
  confidence = field_fct("How clear the answer is.", .levels = c("low", "medium", "high"))
)
```

```{r prompt_fn}
make_prompt <- function(occupation) {
  llm_message(glue(
    'You code survey answers into occupation groups.
     Use only the codebook below. Choose the single best group.
     If the answer names no occupation, use 99.

     Codebook:
     {codebook}

     Survey answer: "{occupation}"'
  ))
}
```

One call looks like this:

```{r one_call, eval = FALSE}
make_prompt("Doin' the numbers") |>
  chat(claude(.model = "claude-sonnet-5-5", .json_schema = occ_schema)) |>
  get_reply_data()
```

A strict answer format can lower accuracy on hard cases (Tam et al., 2024). The rationale field gives the model room to reason; Step 6 measures the result.

### Repeated `chat()` runs, as a comparison

Repeated `chat()` runs fit tasks that need a written reason for each row. We ask Claude Sonnet 5.5 three times for each of 150 sampled answers and keep every run, naming each task with the answer ID and run number so the results stay linked.

```{r repeat_tasks, eval = FALSE}
k <- 3

sample_df <- distinct_occupations |>
  slice_sample(n = 150)

tasks <- sample_df |>
  cross_join(tibble(run = seq_len(k))) |>
  mutate(task_id = paste(id, run, sep = "__"))

llms <- tasks$occupation |>
  map(make_prompt) |>
  set_names(tasks$task_id)
```

```{r repeat_run, eval = FALSE}
replies <- parallel_chat(
  llms,
  claude(.model = "claude-sonnet-5-5", .json_schema = occ_schema),
  .max_active = 4
)
write_rds(replies, "runs_claude.rds")
```

Failed requests do not stop the call. `parallel_chat()` warns how many failed, and the failed elements of the list hold the error condition instead of a message. The extraction below turns those into missing values, so no row disappears silently.

```{r tidy_runs, eval = FALSE}
extract_run <- function(reply) {
  if (!inherits(reply, "tidyllm::LLMMessage")) {
    return(tibble(rationale = NA_character_, occ2 = NA_character_, confidence = NA_character_))
  }
  as_tibble(get_reply_data(reply))
}

runs <- map(replies, extract_run) |>
  bind_rows(.id = "task_id") |>
  separate(task_id, c("id", "run"), sep = "__", convert = TRUE) |>
  rename(label = occ2)
```

The saved results of this run hold three labels for each of the 150 sampled answers.

```{r load_runs}
sample_df <- read_rds("classifier_sample.rds")
runs      <- read_rds("classifier_runs.rds")
run_meta  <- read_rds("classifier_runs_meta.rds")

runs |>
  left_join(sample_df, by = "id") |>
  select(id, occupation, run, label, confidence) |>
  print(n = 6)
```

The token counts of the 450 calls come from the response metadata of each call. The codebook is part of every request, so the prompt is much longer than the answer it labels.

```{r tokens}
tibble(
  calls                = nrow(run_meta$tokens),
  prompt_tokens        = sum(run_meta$tokens$input_tokens),
  completion_tokens    = sum(run_meta$tokens$output_tokens),
  prompt_per_call      = round(mean(run_meta$tokens$input_tokens)),
  completion_per_call  = round(mean(run_meta$tokens$output_tokens))
)
```

```{r vote}
vote <- runs |>
  filter(!is.na(label)) |>
  count(id, label, name = "votes") |>
  group_by(id) |>
  arrange(desc(votes), .by_group = TRUE) |>
  summarise(
    n_runs     = sum(votes),
    majority   = first(label),
    agreement  = first(votes) / sum(votes),
    candidates = paste(label, collapse = "/"),
    .groups    = "drop"
  ) |>
  left_join(sample_df, by = "id") |>
  mutate(unstable = agreement < 1)

vote |>
  count(unstable) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n))
```

The three runs chose the same label for 147 of 150 answers; the majority label supplies Claude's comparison row in the Step 3 and Step 6 tables. Krippendorff's alpha summarises agreement across runs, and the base R function below gives 0.983.

```{r alpha}
kripp_nominal <- function(m) {
  m  <- m[, colSums(!is.na(m)) >= 2, drop = FALSE]
  lv <- sort(unique(as.vector(m)))
  o  <- matrix(0, length(lv), length(lv))
  for (j in seq_len(ncol(m))) {
    v   <- m[, j]
    v   <- v[!is.na(v)]
    tab <- table(factor(v, lv))
    o   <- o + (tab %o% tab - diag(tab)) / (length(v) - 1)
  }
  n <- sum(o)
  1 - (n - 1) * (n - sum(diag(o))) / (n^2 - sum(rowSums(o)^2))
}

runs |>
  select(run, id, label) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = id, values_from = label) |>
  select(-run) |>
  as.matrix() |>
  kripp_nominal() |>
  round(3)
```

### A second pass with a stronger model

The rows that need a second look are the ones where the runs disagreed or where any run said "low". That is a small, concentrated set, which makes a second pass affordable. Instead of voting again with the same prompt, change the task: show the model the answer, the labels the first runs produced and their rationales, and ask for a decision with a stronger setting. Here we use a more capable model with reasoning turned on.

The review pass below uses the earlier flag (runs that disagreed or a confidence word of low); the `decide()` flag of Step 4 is a variant that marks 23 of the 60 answers, of which 3 were in the earlier review set.

For a large flagged set, `send_batch()` sends all requests together; results come back when the batch has finished and cost half as much.

```{r reclassify_prompt}
make_review_prompt <- function(occupation, rationales) {
  llm_message(glue(
    'Earlier independent attempts coded this survey answer; they disagreed or were unsure.
     Decide using the codebook. If the answer is genuinely too vague to place, use 99.

     Codebook:
     {codebook}

     Survey answer: "{occupation}"

     Earlier labels and reasons:
     {rationales}'
  ))
}
```

```{r reclassify_run, eval = FALSE}
any_low <- runs |>
  group_by(id) |>
  summarise(any_low = any(confidence == "low"))

to_review <- vote |>
  left_join(any_low, by = "id") |>
  filter(unstable | any_low) |>
  left_join(
    runs |>
      group_by(id) |>
      summarise(rationales = paste0("- ", label, ": ", rationale, collapse = "\n")),
    by = "id"
  )

review_llms <- map2(to_review$occupation, to_review$rationales, make_review_prompt) |>
  set_names(to_review$id)

review_replies <- parallel_chat(
  review_llms,
  claude(
    .model      = "claude-opus-5-5",
    .json_schema = occ_schema,
    .thinking   = TRUE,
    .max_tokens = 4000
  ),
  .max_active = 4
)

reviewed <- map(review_replies, extract_run) |>
  bind_rows(.id = "id") |>
  transmute(
    id                = as.integer(id),
    review_label      = occ2,
    review_rationale  = rationale,
    review_confidence = confidence
  )
```

Keep `.max_tokens` generous when reasoning is on; the thinking tokens count against it.

```{r reclassify_load}
reviewed <- read_rds("classifier_reviewed.rds")

any_low <- runs |>
  group_by(id) |>
  summarise(any_low = any(confidence == "low"))

to_review <- vote |>
  left_join(any_low, by = "id") |>
  filter(unstable | any_low)

tibble(
  flagged_rows       = nrow(to_review),
  runs_disagreed     = sum(to_review$unstable),
  only_low_confidence = sum(!to_review$unstable),
  reviewed_rows      = nrow(reviewed),
  same_ids           = setequal(to_review$id, reviewed$id)
)
```

```{r final_labels}
final <- vote |>
  left_join(reviewed, by = "id") |>
  left_join(gold, by = "id") |>
  mutate(
    occ2   = coalesce(review_label, majority),
    source = case_when(
      !is.na(review_label) & review_confidence == "low" ~ "human_queue",
      !is.na(review_label)                              ~ "reviewed",
      TRUE                                              ~ "unanimous"
    )
  )

final |> count(source)
```

The review changed the label of a few rows:

```{r review_changes}
final |>
  filter(!is.na(review_label), review_label != majority) |>
  select(occupation, majority, review_label, gold, review_confidence)

tibble(
  changed       = sum(final$review_label != final$majority, na.rm = TRUE),
  reviewed_rows = sum(!is.na(final$review_label))
)
```

The review is a second opinion from the same family of models, so it can repeat a shared misreading. Rows that the reviewer itself marks as low confidence go to a human queue; that is a short list to read by hand.

```{r human_queue}
final |>
  filter(source == "human_queue") |>
  select(occupation, candidates, review_label, gold)
```

## Step 6: Validate against human labels

None of the above tells you whether the labels are right. Only a comparison with human coding does. Draw a random sample of answers, have one or two people code them from the same codebook without seeing the model labels, and resolve their differences. Two rules keep the check honest. The sample must be held out: do not take the codebook examples from it, and do not tune the codebook on it and then report the same sample as your accuracy. And draw it at random across all answers, not only from the flagged ones, or the estimate will be too pessimistic.

For this article the 150 sampled answers were coded in a first pass with AI assistance and then checked by hand by the maintainer. Code 98 in the original file, used for answers that name no occupation, was recoded to 99 to match the codebook. Comparing the model with these labels turned up four labels where the model was right and the first hand label was wrong; they were corrected before the numbers below. That is a useful result in itself: a validation sample is a measurement too, and it has errors that the comparison can surface.

Accuracy and Cohen's kappa come next, computed in base R. Kappa corrects for chance agreement, which matters with 22 groups of very different sizes, where accuracy is dominated by the frequent classes.

```{r metrics}
cohen_kappa <- function(truth, estimate) {
  lv <- sort(unique(c(truth, estimate)))
  tb <- table(factor(truth, lv), factor(estimate, lv))
  po <- sum(diag(tb)) / sum(tb)
  pe <- sum(rowSums(tb) * colSums(tb)) / sum(tb)^2
  (po - pe) / (1 - pe)
}

first_run <- runs |>
  filter(run == 1) |>
  select(id, first_run = label) |>
  inner_join(gold, by = "id")

bind_rows(
  tibble(
    pipeline = "first run only",
    accuracy = mean(first_run$first_run == first_run$gold),
    kappa    = cohen_kappa(first_run$gold, first_run$first_run)
  ),
  tibble(
    pipeline = "majority of 3 runs",
    accuracy = mean(final$majority == final$gold),
    kappa    = cohen_kappa(final$gold, final$majority)
  ),
  tibble(
    pipeline = "majority plus review",
    accuracy = mean(final$occ2 == final$gold),
    kappa    = cohen_kappa(final$gold, final$occ2)
  )
) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

The three rows are close. Voting over three runs and the review pass move the accuracy only slightly, because the model gave the same label in nearly all runs to begin with. The review only touches the flagged rows, and those are the hardest answers, so the gain there starts from a low base:

```{r review_effect}
final |>
  filter(!is.na(review_label)) |>
  summarise(rows = n(), before_review = mean(majority == gold), after_review = mean(occ2 == gold))
```

The table compares accuracy on the same 60 answers: Claude's first run, majority of three runs, and majority plus review each get 50 right; `openai()` and `jev()` get 52, and `gemini()` gets 50. Four of the 60 answers were in the earlier review set.

```{r same_sixty}
claude_sixty <- bind_rows(
  first_run |> filter(id %in% items$id) |> transmute(pipeline = "claude, first run", label = first_run, gold),
  final     |> filter(id %in% items$id) |> transmute(pipeline = "claude, majority of 3 runs", label = majority, gold),
  final     |> filter(id %in% items$id) |> transmute(pipeline = "claude, majority plus review", label = occ2, gold)
)

decide_sixty <- decide_runs |>
  bind_rows(.id = "pipeline") |>
  transmute(pipeline = paste0(pipeline, "()"), label, gold)

bind_rows(claude_sixty, decide_sixty) |>
  group_by(pipeline) |>
  summarise(answers = n(), correct = sum(label == gold), accuracy = round(mean(label == gold), 3))
```

```{r review_overlap}
tibble(
  in_earlier_review_set         = sum(items$id %in% to_review$id),
  flagged_and_in_earlier_review = sum(flags$flagged & flags$id %in% to_review$id)
)
```

With only 60 answers, a difference of two or three answers is within chance, so the methods cannot be told apart. The chunk below computes one standard error for an accuracy of 0.85 across 60 answers.

```{r se}
round(sqrt(0.85 * 0.15 / 60), 3)
```

About one answer in six does not match the human label. Part of the errors sit in the flagged rows and part in rows where the model was unanimous:

```{r errors_by_source}
final |>
  group_by(source) |>
  summarise(answers = n(), mismatches = sum(occ2 != gold), accuracy = mean(occ2 == gold))
```

Where do the mismatches come from?

```{r mismatches}
final |>
  filter(occ2 != gold) |>
  arrange(gold) |>
  select(occupation, model = occ2, human = gold, candidates) |>
  print(n = 30)
```

The same answers fail with all or most decision models: "Barster" and "Private dick" are wrong for all three, with human labels of 99; "Keep things organized" and "Workforce Optimization" are wrong for two of three, though humans assigned them a group. The errors fall into two groups. The first is vague answers such as "Keep things organized", "Workforce Optimization" or "Buildin and fixin things", where the model chose 99 because the codebook says to prefer 99 over a guess, while the human coder placed the answer in a group from context. The second is the opposite: slang or terse answers such as "Private dick", "I haul" and "Barster", where the model guessed a group and the human coded 99. Between them sit real codebook ambiguities: whether bakery work is production (51) or food service (35), where "Lead mechanic supervisor" belongs, and whether massage is healthcare or personal care.

None of these is random noise that more runs would average away. Most of the mismatches are rows where the model gave the same label every time, which is why the repetition in step 5 cannot find them. They are a mix of questions about what the codebook should say and answers that no coder could place with confidence.

When you compare a model with human coders, compare it with the agreement between two humans on the same sample. If two careful coders only agree 0.85 with each other, a model at 0.85 is not failing; the categories are fuzzy. The model is one more coder whose reliability you estimate, and the evidence so far is that its quality depends on the task, the codebook and the data, so it has to be checked each time (Gilardi, Alizadeh and Kubli, 2023; Pangakis, Wolken and Fasching, 2023). Here only one human checked the labels, so that comparison is not possible, and the 83% should be read with that limit in mind.

Check also whether errors are spread evenly. If one group, one kind of respondent or one phrasing carries most of them, a downstream estimate that uses these labels can be biased even when overall accuracy looks high. Where the labels feed a regression or a share estimate, the validation sample can also be used to correct for misclassification instead of only reporting it.

```{r errors_by_group}
final |>
  group_by(human_group = gold) |>
  summarise(answers = n(), accuracy = mean(occ2 == gold)) |>
  arrange(accuracy, desc(answers)) |>
  slice_head(n = 8)
```

## Step 7: Do not tune the codebook on your validation sample

The mismatch table invites an obvious next step: edit the codebook so that these answers come out right. We tried it. Based on the mismatches above, version 2 of the codebook adds a rule for bakery and food batch work (51 unless it is retail counter work), puts massage under personal care (39), says that lead and supervisor titles and general operations work count as management (11), and counts electrical and mechanical upkeep as installation and repair (49). The 150 answers were labelled again three times with the new codebook.

```{r codebook_v2_run, eval = FALSE}
codebook_v2 <- read_file("classifier_codebook_v2.txt") |> trimws()

make_prompt_v2 <- function(occupation) {
  llm_message(glue(
    'You code survey answers into occupation groups.
     Use only the codebook below. Choose the single best group.
     If the answer names no occupation, use 99.

     Codebook:
     {codebook_v2}

     Survey answer: "{occupation}"'
  ))
}

replies_v2 <- tasks$occupation |>
  map(make_prompt_v2) |>
  set_names(tasks$task_id) |>
  parallel_chat(
    claude(.model = "claude-sonnet-5-5", .json_schema = occ_schema),
    .max_active = 4
  )
```

On the sample the edit was written from, version 2 looks better:

```{r codebook_v2_sample}
majority_label <- function(x) names(which.max(table(x)))

runs_v2 <- read_rds("classifier_runs_v2.rds")

sample_comparison <- bind_rows(
  runs    |> group_by(id) |> summarise(label = majority_label(label)) |> mutate(codebook = "v1"),
  runs_v2 |> group_by(id) |> summarise(label = majority_label(label)) |> mutate(codebook = "v2")
) |>
  inner_join(gold, by = "id") |>
  group_by(codebook) |>
  summarise(answers = n(), accuracy = mean(label == gold))

sample_comparison
```

That gain is not evidence that the new codebook is better, because we wrote the edit while looking at these very errors. To find out, we took 292 further distinct answers with human labels that were not in the sample and labelled each once with each codebook.

```{r codebook_heldout_run, eval = FALSE}
heldout_tasks <- heldout |>
  cross_join(tibble(codebook = c("v1", "v2"))) |>
  mutate(task_id = paste(id, codebook, sep = "__"))
```

```{r codebook_heldout}
heldout_runs <- read_rds("classifier_heldout_runs.rds")
heldout_gold <- read_rds("classifier_heldout_gold.rds") |>
  mutate(gold = ifelse(gold == "98", "99", gold))

heldout_comparison <- heldout_runs |>
  inner_join(select(heldout_gold, id, gold), by = "id") |>
  group_by(codebook) |>
  summarise(answers = n(), accuracy = mean(label == gold))

heldout_comparison
```

On the held-out answers version 2 is no better than version 1; it is slightly worse. The edits fitted the quirks of the 150 answers we looked at. This is the same problem as overfitting a model to a validation set: the sample you tune on stops being a measurement. If you want to improve the codebook, split the human-labelled answers first, tune on one part and report on the other, or label a fresh sample after every round of edits.

## Cost and size

Tokens are billable text pieces, each about three-quarters of a word. Labelling all 2,209 distinct answers once costs about 15 cents with `openai()` or `gemini()` and about 10 cents with `jev()`; three Claude runs over the same answers would cost 23.53 USD. The table uses list prices on 2026-11-13.

```{r route_cost}
per_call <- run_meta$tokens |>
  summarise(prompt = mean(input_tokens), completion = mean(output_tokens))

claude_three_runs <- nrow(distinct_occupations) * 3 *
  (per_call$prompt * 2 + per_call$completion * 10) / 1e6

tibble(
  route               = c("decide() with openai()", "decide() with gemini()", "decide() with jev()", "chat() with Claude, three runs"),
  usd_for_2209_answers = sprintf("%.2f", c(0.15, 0.15, 0.10, claude_three_runs))
)
```

The next table shows tokens per answer and prices per million tokens for each provider, with the final column giving the one-pass price for all 2,209 distinct answers.

```{r decide_cost}
decide_cost <- tibble(
  provider        = c("openai", "gemini", "jev"),
  tokens_each     = c(666, 696, 1053),
  usd_per_million = c(0.10, 0.10, 0.042),
  usd_one_pass    = round(2209 * tokens_each * usd_per_million / 1e6, 2)
)

decide_cost
```

The token table in Step 5 gives the size of one `chat()` request: about 1,400 prompt tokens and about 75 completion tokens, depending on the rationale length. At that size the full dataset would look like this:

```{r scale}
per_call <- run_meta$tokens |>
  summarise(prompt = mean(input_tokens), completion = mean(output_tokens))

price <- c(input = 2, output = 10)

tibble(
  distinct_answers  = nrow(distinct_occupations),
  runs              = 3,
  requests          = distinct_answers * runs,
  prompt_tokens     = round(requests * per_call$prompt),
  completion_tokens = round(requests * per_call$completion),
  usd_standard      = round((prompt_tokens * price[["input"]] + completion_tokens * price[["output"]]) / 1e6, 2),
  usd_batch         = usd_standard / 2
)
```

The prices are those of `claude-sonnet-5-5` on 2026-10-02: 2 USD per million input tokens and 10 USD per million output tokens ([Anthropic pricing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing)). The batch API costs half as much at those rates.

The 450 calls behind this article's three runs cost about 1.60 USD. The second pass with `claude-opus-5-5`, at 4 USD per million input tokens and 20 USD per million output tokens, cost about 0.20 USD; the codebook experiment in Step 7 cost about 3.90 USD.

Check your own estimate with `get_metadata()` on one reply before scaling up. Because the codebook repeats in every request, a provider with prefix caching charges less when the start of the request repeats; put the codebook before the survey answer.

One `decide()` pass over all 2,209 answers costs less than the 0.20 USD the Opus review pass cost on our flagged rows. Run `decide()` on the full set, then reserve the stronger model for flagged rows.

## What to take away

- A decision model returns a label and a probability in one call; use `decide()` when the answer is one of a fixed list.
- Put the codebook into `.level_descriptions` and add one line saying what the text is; on our sample the framing line alone lifted `openai()` from 0.57 to 0.87.
- Use the probability to rank rows: below 0.8 the answers were right in 60 to 70 percent of cases, at or above it in 90 to 92 percent.
- A second provider is the cheap second opinion; the three agreed on 49 of 60 answers and were right on 94 percent of those.
- Keep `chat()` for reasons, free labels, files and a stronger model on the hard rows.
- Agreement is not accuracy: validate on a random, held-out, human-coded sample and report how many coders are behind it.
- Do not tune the codebook on the sample you validate with.

The [decision models article](https://edubruell.github.io/tidyllm/articles/tidyllm_decision_models.html) covers yes/no and score questions, more than one question per call, and the providers in detail.
